summary: This Wikipedia article describes Mount Pelée, an active stratovolcano at the northern end of Martinique in the Lesser Antilles. It covers the volcano's geological history in three phases, the catastrophic 1902 eruption that destroyed Saint-Pierre, its 1929–1932 eruption, its recent 2020 alert-level increase, its biology and bird habitat, its 2023 UNESCO World Heritage listing, and its appearances in literature.
one_line: Mount Pelée is an active stratovolcano on Martinique whose 1902 eruption destroyed Saint-Pierre and whose 2023 UNESCO listing protects it.
key_facts: Mount Pelée is an active volcano at the northern end of Martinique, an island and French overseas department in the Lesser Antilles Volcanic Arc.
The 1902 eruption destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre, killing 29,000 to 30,000 people in a few minutes, the worst volcanic disaster of the 20th century.
The main eruption on 8 May 1902 left only three known survivors: Ludger Sylbaris, Léon Compère-Léandre, and a young girl named Havivra Da Ifrile.
Ludger Sylbaris survived because he was in a poorly ventilated, dungeon-like jail cell.
Léon Compère-Léandre, living on the edge of the city, escaped with severe burns.
The Étang Sec caldera formed about three thousand years ago, following a large pumice eruption, and the 1902 eruption took place within the Étang Sec crater.
Mount Pelée erupted again starting 16 September 1929, and the activity ended in late 1932.
On December 6, 2020, the Martinique Volcano Observatory (MVO) raised Mount Pelée's alert level to Yellow [Restless] from Green [Normal].
The 2020 alert followed an increase in seismicity under the volcano beginning in April 2019 and tremors observed the previous month.
Mount Pelée was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on September 16, 2023, together with the pitons of northern Martinique.
The volcanic mountain range represents 12% of Martinique's territory.
The Martinique volcano frog, Allobates chalcopis, is endemic to Mount Pelée.
A 9,262 ha largely forested tract encompassing the mountain is recognised as an Important Bird Area by BirdLife International.
Mount Pelée's cone is composed of stratified layers of hardened ash and solidified lava, and more than 30 eruptions have been identified during the last 5,000 years.
The volcano's elevation is 1,397 m (4,583 ft).
